paragraphs.text: Commentary § 6.8:1 Rule 6.8 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.8. 1. Overview In Gow Estate (Re), 2021 ABQB 305, 2021 CarswellAlta 962, Justice Feth gave this overview of the Rule: [14] Rule 6.8 is similar to its predecessor, Rule 266. The rule finds its origins in a longstanding practice in Canadian and British civil courts allowing for the collection of evidence from individuals, including partie s, who cannot or will not provide affidavit evidence for motions: Dechant v Law Society of Alberta, 2000 ABCA 265 at paras 12–14 [Dechant]. [15] Numerous principles circumscribe the scope and manner of such questioning, including: a. The information sought must be relevant and material to the pending motion: Dechant at para 17; Alberta Treasury Branches v Leahy, 1999 ABQB 842 at paras 20–26 [Leahy]; Robertson v Edmonton (City) Police Service (#6), 2003 ABQB 188 at para 13, aff'd 2003 ABCA 279; AP v SP, 2017 ABQB 672 at para 15; b. The questioning is not an examination for discovery and a fishing expedition is not permitted: Leahy at para 22; c. Parties adverse in interest can be examined: Rule 6.20(2); Ferguson v Cairns (1959), 1959 CanLII 279 (AB CA), 21 DLR (2d) 659 at 662, [1959] 30 WWR 276 (Alta CA) [Ferguson]; d. The questioning party usually conducts an examination-in-chief of the witness and cannot cross-examine, but unlike the predecessor rule, cross-examination is permitted of parties adverse in interest: Dechant at para 15; Rule 6.20(2); Precision Drilling Canada Limited v Yangarra Resources Ltd, 2013 ABQB 492 at paras 30, 37-38, 49, 54; e. The witness may also be questioned by any other party and may then be questioned again by the party who summoned the witness: Rule 6.20(1); f. All of the evidence obtained at the questioning is placed before the judge hearing the application and forms part of the case of the party who summoned the witness: Dechant at para 15; Ferguson at 662; g. To the extent a witness is directed to produce records for the questioning, the notice must identify the records sought with as much precision as is fair and feasible, much like a subpoena duces tecum, and the records must be relevant to the pending application: Apotex Inc v Alberta (1996), 1996 CanLII 10361 (AB QB), 182 AR 321, 38 Alta LR (3d) 153 at paras 38-39; Leahy at paras 24–26; h. The Court may regulate the questioning for abuse of process, including whether the application itself is an abuse of process: Dechant at para 14; i. The Court may order the witness to attend for questioning and to bring records to the questioning: Rule 6.38; and j. The Court may provide directions in advance of the questioning on the scope of permissible questions: Dechant at para 16. In Guillevin International Co. v. Barry, 2022 ABCA 144, 2022 CarswellAlta 986, the Court of Appeal gave this summary of the Rule: [34]… The transcripts of an examination under R. 6.8 would all have been admissible evidence. The examiner is not permitted to just “read in” those portions of the transcript that it finds to be supportive of its case. Further, this would not just be evidence against Schwanke, but would be evidence for or against all the parties. [35] Any party has a prima facie right to examine a witness under R. 6.8 without consent or court order. Obtaining evidence from a recalcitrant witness supports the court's truth-seeking function, and is exactly what the rule is for: Neill v Millar, 2021 ABQB 305 at paras. 12–14, 48-49. There is no objection to examining an opposing party under the rule; a party in a civil action has no right to “stand silent”: Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co v Schneider, 1995 ABCA 419 at paras. 13-14, 34 Alta LR (3d) 1, 174 AR 304; Ferguson v Cairns (1959), 1959 CanLII 279 (AB CA), 21 DLR (2d) 659, 30 WWR 276 (Alta SC, App Div). While a chambers judge can set aside such an appointment if it is an abuse of process, the burden of showing an abuse is on the witness. The appointment should not be set aside unless there are no more proportionate remedies. On this record there was no sufficient reason for the chambers judge to set aside the notice under R. 6.8. 2. Equitable Principle of Discovery not Displaced (Norwich Applications) In Interclaim Holdings Ltd. v. Down (2000), 80 Alta. L.R. (3d) 248 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Kent discussed the equitable principle of discovery. She concluded that it still exists in Alberta, and was not displaced by Rule 266. That comment would seem to also apply to Rule 6.8. Of particular interest is her discussion of the right of discovery in equity (as opposed to a right of discovery granted by the Rules). At pp. 250-253, Her Ladyship said: I start the juridical analysis with [Norwich Pharmacal Co. v. Customs & Excise Commissioners (1973), [1974] A.C. 133 (U.K. H.L.)]. Norwich Pharmacal believed that someone was importing drugs for which Norwich had the patent. It wanted to bring legal proceedings against the importers but did not know thier identity. The Customs office did know the identity but refused to provide that information. The House of Lords acknowledged that the right of discovery is founded in equity. The Law Lords held that although there was no broad independent right of discovery against a person who had committed no wrong or was a mere witness, there could be discovery where without the discovery no action could be commenced against a wrongdoer and where the person from whom discovery was sought had been innocently involved in the wrongdoing. They said that since discovery itself is an equitable remedy, this limited type of discovery remained nothwithstanding the clarification of civil practice by the introduction of rules of practice. … All of this leads me to conclude that, absent a rule of practice which overrides, in equity there is a right of third party pre-action discovery. … … While Rules 209 and 266 provide for pre-trial discovery of documents and witnesses, they do not deal with pre-action discovery to determine identity or trace assets of an alleged wrongdoer. These rules have not replaced the equitable principle of discovery in such circumstances … … Because of the dangers of granting ex parte relief, such orders should be granted only where there is a strong prima facie case. … Given the intrusive nature of such orders and the loss of confidentiality of someone who is only a potential defendant, I cannot emphasize too much the need for a strong case. … Where the order is sought to preserve assets, the object must be limited to that purpose and not to help build the plaintiff's case before the action is even started. While it may be sometimes difficult to determine the difference, the tracing sought to be done through an order must only be to freeze assets to prevent their removal from the jurisdiction. In Alberta Treasury Branches v. Leahy, 2000 ABQB 575, 2000 CarswellAlta 1648, 270 A.R. 1; affirmed 2002 ABCA 101, 2002 CarswellAlta 578, 303 A.R. 63, 51 Alta. L.R. (4th) 94; leave to appeal refused 2002 CarswellAlta 1510, 327 A.R. 120 (note) (S.C.C.), Mr. Justice Mason also considered the equitable relief of bill of discovery. At pp. 25-26, he said: The jurisdiction of the court to grant such relief is based on the ancient equitable bill of discovery which was the subject of renewed interest in a series of cases starting with Norwich. A concise summary of the remedy is contained in Stone, J.A.'s, judgment in Glaxco Wellcome plc v. Minister of National Revenue, [1998] 4 F.C. 439, 228 N.R. 164 (F.C.A.), at 458 (footnote references omitted): The equitable bill of discovery is in essence a form of pre-action discovery. It is of ancient origin. It developed alongside the procedures for discovery which are ordinarily available in the course of litigation and which, it is worth noting, also originated in the courts of equity. This remedy permits a court, acting through its equitable jurisdiction, to order discovery of a person against whom the applicant for the bill of discovery has no cause of action and who is not a party to contemplated litigation. While it appears that an independent action for discovery cannot be brought against a person who is in the position of a ‘mere witness’ or bystander to the cause of action, the case law suggests that a bill of discovery may be issued against an individual who is in some way connected to or involved in the misconduct. In Norwich, the appellant pharmaceutical companies/laboratory were the owners and licensees of a patent for a chemical compound. The appellants believed their patent was being infringed by illicit importations of the compound manufactured abroad. In order to determine the names and addresses of the alleged importers, an action was brought against the Commissioners of Customs and Excise (“CCE”) alleging patent infringement and seeking orders to disclose the information. Ultimately the appellants abandoned the infringement claim against CCE and the appeal proceeded on the basis that it was an action for discovery only. Graham, J., ordered CCE to disclose the information. The Court of Appeal reversed that decision and the House of Lords allowed the appeal. Lord Reid referred to the review of the case authorities in the area by Lords Cross and Kilbrandon and stated at 175: They seem to me to point to a very reasonable principle that if through no fault of his own a person gets mixed up in the tortious acts of others so as to facilitate their wrongdoing he may incur no personal liability but he comes under a duty to assist the person who has been wronged by giving him full information and disclosing the identity of the wrongdoers. I do not think that it matters whether he became so mixed up by voluntary action on his part or because it was his duty to do what he did. (emphasis added) The House of Lords established threshold requirements for obtaining a bill of discovery: the applicants must have a bona fide claim against the alleged wrongdoers; it may not be issued against a mere witness or disinterested bystander to the alleged misconduct and the person from whom discovery is sought must be the only practical source of information available. The Courts in both England and Canada have extended the equitable remedy of discovery as revitalized by Norwich to combat the stratagems and chameleon antics of fraudsters. The principles have been further extended and applied to numerous subsequent cases so as to not only identify wrongdoers but to trace funds and assets and even to assist a prospective plaintiff in determining whether a cause of action exists. The evolution of the remedy has focussed on the extension and development of the “full information” portion of the relief as opposed to simply discovering the identity of the wrongdoer. This largely occurred in actions to trace funds fraudulently taken or mistakenly misappropriated and then wrongfully withheld. After reviewing the use of the bill of discovery by other Canadian courts, Mason J. considered its use in Alberta. At pp. 34-35, his Lordship said: The remedy is not precluded by the Alberta Rules of Court. As WEM [defendant] recognized in its submissions on these applications, while the Rules do provide for limited pre-trial examination and production of documents from non-parties, they do not contemplate the particular remedies at issue here. In any event, I agree with the reasoning of Saunders, J., and am persuaded that Alberta judges can reach behind the Alberta Rules of Court and exercise fully the broader procedural remedies of the equitable bill of discovery. The foregoing review demonstrates that: a. Norwich-type relief has been granted in varied situations: (i) where the information sought is necessary to identify wrongdoers; (ii) to find and preserve evidence that may substantiate or support an action against either known or unknown wrongdoers, or even determine whether an action exists; and (iii) to trace and preserve assets. b. The court will consider the following factors on an application for Norwich relief: (i) Whether the applicant has provided evidence sufficient to raise a valid, bona fide or reasonable claim; (ii)Whether the applicant has established a relationship with the third party from whom the information is sought such that it establishes that the third party is somehow involved in the acts complained of; (iii) Whether the third party is the only practicable source of the information available; (iv) Whether the third party can be indemnified for costs to which the third party may be exposed because of the disclosure, some refer to the associated expenses of complying with the orders, while others speak of damages; and (v) Whether the interests of justice favour the obtaining of the disclosure. McMahon J., in Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corp. v. EFA Software Services Ltd., 2001 ABQB 425, 2001 CarswellAlta 674, 294 A.R. 182, at pp. 191-192, agreed with Mason J. Mason J. also concluded that the implied undertaking of confidentiality which applies to examinations for discovery does not apply to Norwich examinations. At p. 79, his Lordship said: Proceedings within the principles of Norwich, as I have found these to be, generally contemplate that the information obtained will be used in another action or against additional parties. The courts have accordingly recognized that the implied undertaking does not even arise in those circumstances. In B. (A.) v. D. (C.), 2007 ABQB 516, 2007 CarswellAlta 1091, 426 A.R. 352, 78 Alta. L.R. (4th) 327, Veit J. had before her an ex parte application for “a Norwich-type order requiring five named financial institutions to provide to the applicant all of the banking records held with each institution by the defendant, C.D., and by nine other named individuals and persons who [were] not parties” in the action. The order sought would also provide that none of the persons would be told that their banking records had been requisitioned. Her Ladyship denied the application, and her reasons for doing so are instructive on the issue of what must be established in order to obtain a Norwich-type of order. At pp. 329-330, Veit J. said: 3 This application departs considerably from the original Norwich situation: here, the plaintiff has started proceedings against the defendant, whom it clearly considers to be the ultimate wrongdoer, and is entitled to standard discovery of that party. The financial records of the defendant, to which the plaintiff is entitled under standard discovery processes, are likely to supply to the plaintiff any additional fact “crucial to the proper allegation” of the defendant's liability. In other words, here the plaintiff/applicant does not require equitable discovery. 4 The further an application departs from the original Norwich equitable discovery mechanism, the more closely a court must assess each of the requirements to make an order for equitable discovery. For example, it is understandable that, in the original Norwich situation and in closely comparable situations, the applicant need only establish a bona fide claim, it being the expectation that the information requested was only needed to start proceedings against a wrongdoer. However, where, as here, the plaintiff appears to be attempting, at least in part, to obtain secret discovery of a known defendant with a view to freezing or preserving funds, the level of proof of the claim must rise to the level required of pre-judgment garnishment applications. … 6 In any event, the applicant has not met the tests required by Canadian case law with respect to the issuance of a Norwich-type order: it has not provided evidence sufficient to raise a valid, bona fide, claim against any persons other than persons who are already known to the plaintiff and with respect to whom the plaintiff is in a position to commence, or already has commenced, legal proceedings. The applicant has not provided adequate proof of the validity of its claim against the defendant to entitle it to pre-trial freezing of the defendant's assets; it has not established that the financial institutions which are the immediate subjects of this applicant, are somehow involved in, or somehow participated in, the acts of which the plaintiff complains, and therefore more than mere witnesses to any alleged fraud; it has not established that the financial institutions are the only practicable source of the information it is requesting. On the contrary, the applicant's own lawyers are presumably the best source of background information about several of the specific allegations made; it can, and presumably does, indemnify the financial institutions for both the costs which they would incur and any damages sustained, although such damages are unlikely to be incurred in complying with the terms of this order. Had the order requested been granted, clarification of the applicant's undertaking would have been required to ensure that damages, as well as costs, came within the ambit of the undertaking; the interests of justice do not favour the granting of the order. The type of order requested is exceptional and the court should only exercise its discretion to grant such an order when it is satisfied that it is necessary to do so. Among the factors considered, whereas a low degree of confidentiality attached to the names of the wrongdoers in the Norwich situation, here, a high degree of confidentiality attaches to banking records. This is not a situation where the potential to set aside the orders could redress a just balance amongst the persons affected; even if affected parties could move to set aside the orders, the invasion of the privacy of the clients of the target institutions would have been irretrievably breached. In the circumstances, the applicant's request amounts to a request for a fishing licence. Also, the long delay between the dates of the alleged wrongdoing and the date of the application make it unlikely that the requested order could provide any actual relief to the plaintiff. An appeal to the Court of Appeal of Alberta was dismissed (see: B. (A.) v. D. (C.), 2008 ABCA 51, 2008 CarswellAlta 169, 429 A.R. 89, 85 Alta. L.R. (4th) 18. The Court of Appeal said, at paras. 15-16: 15 It must be remembered that the Norwich order—like other forms of pre-trial discovery or execution processes—has been considered somewhat draconian in effect: Design Group Staffing Inc. v. Fierlbeck, [2006] A.J. No. 538 at para. 8 per Slatter J. (as he then was). Therefore, the discretion to grant such orders must be exercised cautiously. Although Lord Denning in British Steel Corp. v. Granada Television Ltd., [1981] 1 All ER 417 at page 439 characterized the decision in Norwich Pharmacal as having “opened a new chapter in our law”, he warned in Bankers Trust Co. v. Shapira, [1980] 3 All ER 353 at p. 357, that “[t]his new jurisdiction must, of course, be carefully exercised.” We agree. 16 The most important point for the purposes of this appeal is that a Norwich order is not intended as a device to circumvent the normal discovery process which can effectively achieve the same result. The investigative capacity of Norwich orders was applied in Ashworth Hospital Authority v. MNG Ltd., [2002] 1 W.L.R. 2033 (H.L.) in circumstances of necessity, sufficiency of grounds and proportionality. The Chambers Judge here was alive to these legitimate concerns.… When considering the judgment of Veit J., one should keep in mind the Court of Appeal's other comment (at para. 7): …In light of our view of the outcome here, it is not necessary for us to explore a number of aspects of the judgment of the chambers judge exploring the conditions precedent to the granting of a Norwich order and the scope of such orders and we decline to do so. 3. Abuse of Process However, within a rule 266 application, one must review the possibility that there has been abuse of process. The history of this lawsuit is long and convoluted. There have been long periods of inaction by the appellant and indeed, his action was struck for want of prosecution. There has been a failure by the appellant on a number of occasions and on a number of bases to pursue his remedies expeditiously in ways available to him. We note, for example, the possibility of there having been an examination under rule 244 or under rule 266 for the hearing before the Master. Having said that, we must consider that the conduct of litigation is in the hands of the lawyers. The rules are designed to allow counsel to develop their cases and to prepare evidence for hearings before the court, hearings such as the Queen's Bench hearing which will take place as a de novo hearing. We are not able to say that there was an abuse of process in this case. Richardson v. Honeywell Ltd. (1996), 181 A.R. 247 (C.A.), at 250, per Picard J. 4. The Evidence Is that of the Examiner [Rule 266] is a rule strengthening the adversary process. This is not a criminal proceeding with the right of an accused to remain silent. The respondent can and did choose not to file any evidence and that is his option. But R. 266 permits the appellant to seek evidence from him with the proviso that it becomes the evidence of the examiner. Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co. v. Schneider (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.), at 4, per curiam. 5. The Rule permits cross-examination by the party calling the witness In Precision Drilling Canada Ltd. v. Yangarra Resources Ltd., 2013 ABQB 492, 2013 CarswellAlta 1723, 570 A.R. 77, 85 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraphs 37-38: 37 With these interpretive principles in mind, and for the reasons that follow, I conclude that Rule 6.8 is sufficiently broad to permit cross-examination of a witness by the party calling that witness without the traditional necessity of an intervening declaration of hostility. If that were not so, a party seeking to cross-examine a witness in circumstances such as these would have to apply to a Master for permission to call the witness and then make a separate application to a Justice for a declaration that the witness is hostile, since the Master has no jurisdiction to make such a declaration. The Court of Appeal in Ferguson held at p 279 that “… if a party can ever be declared a hostile witness, he can only be so declared by a Judge.” This statement was adopted by Master Breitkreuz in 274099 Alberta Ltd v. West Edmonton Mall Shopping Centre Ltd. (1988), 92 AR 232 (QB) where he stated at para 14 that “… a witness can only become a hostile witness by declaration of a judge”. (The Master's decision was reversed by this Court, but restored by the Court of Appeal at (1990), 114 AR 57.) Similarly, in TW v. Alberta (Edmonton and Area Child & Family Services Region 6), 2010 ABQB 505, 497 AR 130, Graesser J. held at para 24 that “I suppose it is possible to have the witness declared hostile, but that would involve a subsequent court application.” Thus, if cross-examination of a witness called by the questioning party is permitted only upon a declaration of hostility, two applications would be required. This separate hostility application contemplates a concurrent real-time examination of the witness as the case proceeds. In other words, even if it is possible, that is still a separate application and this is antithetical to the efficiency sought to be promoted by the new Rules. 38 While I recognize that the language of Rule 6.8 is not perfectly express on this point, I am satisfied that this is the proper interpretation, given the departure from the old Rules represented by the wording of Rule 6.20. It is significant, in my view, that the old Rules drew a distinction between examination on affidavit, which was in the form of cross-examination, and examination of a person called as a witness, which was in the form of direct examination, as it would be at trial. By contrast, Rule 6.20(1) refers to both and appears to draw no distinction between them in respect of the form of examination. In my view, this leaves open the possibility of broader access to cross-examination. 6. Prima Facie Right The applicant in this case prima facie meets the requirements of R. 266 and, according to the principles outlined by the Ontario Court of Appeal in the Can. Metal Co. case, the applicant therefore has a prima facie right to resort to the rule. Fitzpatrick v. Fornier (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 263 (Q.B.), at 265, per Veit J. 7. Use of Rule One cannot abuse the process. The defendants' argument in opposition to the motion is that since it is clear that the plaintiff would be unsuccessful in obtaining discovery of an employee of the defendants' insurance company, the plaintiff cannot do indirectly through R. 266 what she cannot do directly through RR. 200 and 201. In support of that position, they also refer to the Can. Metal Co. case and to Oliverio v. Orsini, [1940] O.W.N. 374 (H.C.), and Carlson v. Carlson (1974), 7 C.P.C. 117 (Ont. Dist. Ct.). Those cases are authority for the proposition that the courts will not allow the rules to be used so as to constitute an abuse of process. In the Can. Metal Co. case, the court said the following at p. 192: The evidence sought to be elicited must be relevant to the issue on the motion. If it is, there is a prima facie right to resort to Rule [266]. That right must not be so exercised as to be an abuse of the process of the Court. There will be such an abuse if the main motion is itself an abuse, as by being frivolous and vexatious, or if the process under Rule [266], while ostensibly for the purpose of eliciting relevant evidence, is in fact being used for an ulterior or improper purpose, or if the process is being used in such a way as to be in itself an abuse (as for example, by issuing subpoenas to every member of the House of Commons to prove a defamatory statement shouted out by a spectator in the gallery). The list is not exhaustive. In the Oliverio decision, the master made the following comments at p. 376: These four persons will all be witnesses at the trial of this action, and the plaintiff contends that the purpose of the motion is to cross-examine them before trial. This is clearly contrary to all accepted principles of practice and amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court. The defendant, by launching this motion, is seeking to obtain the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses: D. v. W. (1912), 3 D.L.R. 293; Rene v. Carling Export Brewing (1927), 61 O.L.R. 495. In the Carlson case, the plaintiff sought an order that a certain person be required to attend for discovery or as a witness prior to trial. It should be noted that the motion in that case does not appear to meet the prerequisites set out in either our R. 266 or, indeed, in the Ontario Rules. The learned trial judge made this comment with respect to that portion of the application at p. 119: It is apparent that Audrey Humphries will be a material witness at the trial of this action and for this reason it is understandable that the plaintiff would want to know what that evidence might be in advance of the trial. He also seeks this information from her because of the defendant's inability to recollect the minute details of the alleged advances of money by way of gift to her from her mother which she alleges went into the original acquisition of the property. The plaintiff has advanced no other reason and has cited no authority for his application for an order that Audrey Humphries be required to attend as a witness or that he be permitted to examine her as a witness prior to trial. Another case not referred to by counsel, but which stands in the same “abuse of process” line of authority, is Morgan v. Morgan (1980), 19 C.P.C 259 (Ont. Div. Ct.), where an application to conduct a second discovery of a party was struck out as an abuse of process. Fitzpatrick v. Fornier (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 263 (Q.B.), at 264-65, per Veit J. In Feeney v. Her Majesty the Queen in the Right of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 255, 2021 CarswellAlta 1655, leave to appeal refused 2022 ABCA 10, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 802 (S.C.C.), Justice Khullar said: [4] To order a witness to submit to questioning under r 6.8, the Court needs to have some sense of the questions that would be asked and whether the witnesses have relevant information to offer: Dechant v Law Society of Alberta, 2000 ABCA 265 at para 16; AP v SP, 2017 ABQB 672 at para 15. … 8. Onus of Proof The onus to prove abuse of process rests on the respondent. As to whether the plaintiff's application in the main motion (or 27th February motion) constitutes an abuse of process of the court, the burden of proof of which appears to me to lie upon the respondent …Fitzpatrick v. Fornier, supra, at 265. In Robertson v. Edmonton Chief of Police, 2003 ABQB 188, 2003 CarswellAlta 283, 334 A.R. 151, Clackson J. explained that a witness wishing to avoid a Notice To Attend under this Rule bears the onus of showing that he or she does not have material or relevant evidence. Likewise, the person causing the Notice To Attend bears the initial onus of showing that there is a basis for the Notice. At p. 154, his Lordship said: I think the court's analysis in Dechant[Dechant v. Law Society of Alberta (2002), 266 A.R. 249 (C.A.)] leads to the conclusion that rule 266 is really like a subpoena. The only difference is the testimony in a rule 266 examination is recorded and given at a place other than a courtroom. It is not surprising that the historic formulation of rule 266 imposes a trial structure on the extra curial evidence. After all that is a structure and process which is very familiar in our adversary system. The limitations on the rule are really the same limitations faced by counsel calling a witness at trial. The witnesses evidence is part of the case of the party that called him or her and the party calling that witness may not lead that witness. The whole of the witness' testimony is evidence subject only to relevance and materiality. Continuing with the analogy, a witness at trial would be compelled to answer all questions seeking relevant and material evidence. It is only questions designed to illicit evidence which is either not relevant or not material that would be precluded. In theory then, rule 266 witnesses should be treated in the same way. If a witness has relevant and material evidence to give then he or she may be examined. None of the foregoing is particularly controversial, but in my view it provides the answer to the threshold dispute. A witness subpoenaed (served with a notice to attend in this jurisdiction) who seeks to avoid that summons has the burden of showing that his evidence is either not relevant or not material. That onus is preceded by an onus on the summonser to establish that there is a basis for the summons. At trial where viva voce testimony is received, the summonser need only establish that the proposed witness' evidence may be relevant and material in order to satisfy the burden upon him and compel the attendance requested. Similarly, any objectionable questions put to such a witness must be allowed if the questions could result in answers which are relevant and material to the issues involved. At p. 155, Clackson J. said: … Of course that does not mean that a rule 266 witness is to be subjected to limitless hectoring on remote matters of little relevance and less materiality. A rule 266 examination is not an examination for discovery either in style or in scope. In my view, the questions asked must be relevant and material and directly or very nearly directly related to an issue, anything else would not be tolerated at trial and is therefore not appropriate under rule 266. To be clear, the determination here is not about whether any particular question is appropriate when measured by the standard of relevance, rather the determination is whether there may be information possessed by the prospective witness which is relevant. At trial a witness must only answer questions designed to get at what is relevant and material. At discovery a witness must answer all questions which may be relevant and material. A rule 266 notice is sound if there is a possibility that the summonsed person will have something of relevance to say on an issue in the proceedings. If there is that possibility, then the summons is sound. If there is not that possibility then the summons is a fishing expedition and therefore an abuse. 9. Effect of Examination I believe that it should be noted in this context that the examination under R. 266 appears to stand quite independently from an examination for discovery; there is no question at this stage of the examination of a witness under R. 266 being considered as the examination of a party on discovery and the answers of this witness will not bind automatically the defendants in the way that the parties' examination for discovery can be used at trial. Fitzpatrick v. Fornier (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 263 at 266 (Q.B.). In Dul v. Dul (1998), 229 A.R. 398 (Q.B.), Burrows J. confirmed that R. 266 is not a mechanism to examine non-parties for discovery. At pp. 399-400, His Lordship said: Rule 266 cannot be used to require a nonparty to submit to discovery. In Simmons v. McKinney, [1994] A.J. No. 25, the Alberta Court of Appeal said: It is axiomatic that only a party can be examined for discovery in Alberta. A mere witness cannot (with narrow exceptions such as auditors and persons employed by a party). An established ground for upsetting an examination under r. 314 or r. 266 is that it is being used as an examination for discovery. … This [application] is clearly an attempt to use rule 266 to obtain discovery. That would be an abuse of the rule. And more recently Master Quinn again stated: Counsel for the defendants submits that in cases where a plaintiff does not file an affidavit in opposition to an application for security for costs, a defendant would have to have examination for discovery of the plaintiff before the application could be made, if an examination pursuant to rule 266 was not possible. Costs of examination for discovery are often substantial. If an order for security for costs is made following an examination for discovery, and the plaintiff is unable to furnish the security the plaintiff's action is doomed, and the costs of the examination for discovery are, in effect, squandered. In Ferguson v. Cairns (1959), 30 W.W.R. (N.S.) 277 (Alta. C.A.), the court considered an appeal on an application for security for costs where the chambers judge had held that the plaintiff could not be compelled to submit to an examination pursuant to rule 317 (now rule 266). The Court of Appeal held such an examination was proper. At page 279 Johnson, J.A., said: It was said that such an examination would amount to an examination for discovery before that stage in the proceedings had been reached, but an examination under this rule is not examination for discovery—any doubt as to this is removed by the closing words of the rule, ‘his examination conducted in the same manner as those of a witness at the trial’. If the opposite party is called, he becomes a witness of the party calling him. He is bound by his testimony to the same extent as he would be bound by the evidence of any witness he might call. He cannot cross-examine him—if a party can ever be declared a hostile witness, he can only be so declared by a judge. The Rules provide for the calling of an opposite party at trial. On principle there would appear to be no reason why his evidence should not be available on a ‘motion, petition or other proceeding before the court.’… Having regard to the Ferguson case I conclude that the examination of the plaintiff pursuant to rule 266 was proper, and that the evidence adduced on the examination is properly admissible on the application for security for costs. Bourassa v. North West Trust Co. (1991), 116 A.R. 281 at 283-84 (Master). 10. Scope of Examination … there can be no doubt that on such examinations, subject to the ordinary rules of evidence, the examining party is entitled to ask all questions which are relevant to the application then pending, and is not to be confined in the scope of his examination by the material which the opposing party chooses to insert in its affidavits used in support of the application. Alberta Pulpwood Exporting Co. v. Falls Paper & Power Co. (1954), 14 W.W.R. 121 (Alta. T.D.), at 127, per Egbert J. In Apotex Inc. v. Alberta (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (Q.B.), Hutchinson J. said at paragraph 37: Rules 266 and 267 appear to encompass the same scope as a subpoena duces tecum. In Seabolt Watershed Assn. v. Brown, 2002 ABQB 183, 2002 CarswellAlta 233, 306 A.R. 377 (Master), the defendants applied for an order under Rule 267 directing the plaintiff to disclose its financial records so that the defendants could use those records in support of a security for costs application under Rule 593. There was no suggestion that the action was frivolous, and therefore an application under Rule 593(1)(g) was not appropriate. The application was denied. Master Breitkreuz held that simply saying that the plaintiff association had not filed any financial statements with the corporate registry fell short of showing that the plaintiff did not have assets. In other words the proven fact (the absence of filed financial statements) did not support the inference sought (a lack of assets). Without some evidence about the state of the plaintiff's financial affairs, there was no evidentiary basis upon which to make an order under Rule 267. At pp. 379-380, the learned Master said: There is another Ontario case which discusses the interplay between their counterparts to our Rules 593 and 267. It is Reiger v. Chief of Police (1987), 58 O.R. (2d) 203 (Ont. Master). The case ultimately turned on another point because the Ontario Public Authorities Protection Act also contains a security for costs provision and the matter was ultimately decided on the interpretation of the relevant section under that statute. But the case is helpful in that it discusses the distinction to be drawn between stating something and showing something. It deals with the level of proof required by an applicant in such an application before the onus shifts to the respondent in rebutting proof ofhis sufficient assets. It may be regrettable that the outcome of this application turns on something as fine as the distinction between state and show, but upon reflexion the distinction does have some substance. It appears to me that when the evidence in support of an application to examine under Rule 267 essentially does nothing more than state that the plaintiff has not filed a financial return, I am entitled to draw the conclusion that nothing has been shown about the plaintiffs' financial affairs. From the cases quote above, it would appear that an examination of a witness under Rule 266 and the production of documents under Rule 267 constitutes a call for testimony and not for discovery under the discovery Rules of Court. Apotex Inc. v. Alberta (1996), 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 at 177 (Q.B.). In Alberta Treasury Branches v. Leahy (1999), 254 A.R. 280 (Q.B.), Mason, J. agreed with Hutchinson, J. At p. 288, Mason. J. said: … I agree with the assessment of Hutchinson, J., that the scope of rules 266 and 267 is akin to a subpoena duces tecum. Similarly the scope of what can be produced in terms of the evidence to be given and the documents produced by an application under these rules is akin to what can be required by a subpoena duces tecum. … In Plamondon v. Plamondon, 2017 ABQB 672, 2017 CarswellAlta 2306, the defendant applied “under rule 6.8 to compel the Plaintiff's former counsel to answer questions.” In relation to Rule 6.8, Justice Kullar said: 15 First, it is important to note that this is not a Norwich type application—where a party is seeking the right to question a person prior to commencing a legal action: The legal test for a Norwich application (including necessity) does not apply in these circumstances. As noted in the commentary under Fradsham's Alberta Rules of Court Annotated 2018, this rule and its predecessor, is similar to a subpoena duces tecum in that a party wishing to examine a witness must establish that the evidence from the witness may be relevant and material in order to compel the witness to attend. The onus is then on the witness to object as to why he or she does not have to attend. Robertson v Edmonton Chief of Police, 2003 ABQB 188 (Clackson, J.) at para 14, aff'd 2003 ABCA 279; Apotex Inc. v Alberta (1966), 38 Alta LR (3d) 153 (at para 65) (Hutchinson, J.). 11. Witnesses examined under R. 6.8 are not required to provide undertakings In Great North Equipment Inc. v. Penney, 2024 ABKB 391, Justice Feasby concluded that a witness examined under Rule 6.8 is not compelled to provide undertakings. He said: [16] There is a fundamental difference between witnesses examined pursuant to Rule 6.7 and Rule 6.8. Witnesses who have sworn an affidavit have consented to taking an active role in the litigation; they are either parties or have agreed to assist a party. It is reasonable to ask such witnesses to answer undertakings in the circumstances stated by Master Prowse in Dow Chemical. Indeed, their choice to provide an affidavit implies their consent to provide information and records referred to in their affidavit and to provide other information that would significantly assist the Court so long as it is not overly onerous to do so. [17] Witnesses who are examined pursuant to Rule 6.8 are strangers to the litigation in the sense that they are not parties. Witnesses examined pursuant to Rule 6.8, as in the present case, have a connection to the events in dispute but, for whatever reason, have not been joined to the litigation as parties. Such witnesses have not consented to taking an active role in the litigation and it is reasonable that they be treated differently than witness who have provided an affidavit. A Rule 6.8 examination should be no more intrusive than necessary – this is a theme that runs through the principles governing Rule 6.8 examinations identified by Feth J, as he then was, in Gow Estate (Re), 2021 ABQB 305 at para 15. …. [19] Maintaining a rule against undertakings in the context of Rule 6.8 balances the interests of litigants in obtaining evidence for their application and the interests of strangers to litigation to minimize their involvement. The rule is also consistent with the principle that the presentation of oral evidence obtained in advance of an application to the Court follows the model for presentation of viva voce evidence in Court on an application or trial. [20] The risk inherent in a rule against requiring undertakings in Rule 6.8 examinations is that witnesses will be deliberately ill-informed and uncooperative. This risk can be addressed through other means. For example, the Court has the power to compel a witness to re-attend for questioning pursuant to Rule 6.38. And, in extreme cases, the contempt power may be used to compel compliance. 12. Application of Rule to Other Statutes In Lac La Biche School Division No. 51 v. Rimar Construction Ltd. (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 398 (Master), Master Breitkreuz used former R. 266 to permit the examination of a non-party in a builder's lien action. He said at p. 400: It appears that an employee or an officer of the bank does not fit within the relevant subsections of s. 24 of the Builders' Lien Act. The bank is assignee of funds payable by subcontractors to the general contractor. I do not believe that the various portions of the Builders' Lien Act are of any assistance to the applicant. However, I believe RR. 266 and 267 of the Rules of Court may be of assistance to the applicant … I believe the Rules of Court can be used to facilitate the procedure under a statute unless the rules are in direct conflict with any provision in the statutes. In St. Denis v. Trumbley (1977), 3 Alta. L.R. (2d) 193 (C.A.) McDermid J.A. said this at p. 198: It would appear to me that, whether the view is taken that the rules are applicable or that the court must regulate its own procedure in the absence of the Minister making rules, the end result is the same. Once it is decided that the procedure is civil the court should turn to the ordinary civil rules governing civil procedure, ie., the Rules of Court. In applying the rules, R. 3 states they are to be applied ‘so far as may be practicable’ and the practicality of applying any rule must be considered in light of the provisions of the Act. In deciding whether a rule contained in the Rules of Court is applicable the court should consider: firstly, whether the rule is to be applied contrary to any provision in the Act or any regulation made by the Minister and, if it is, such rule does not apply; secondly, whether it is practicable to apply the rule and, if it is not, such rule does not apply. I believe that principle applies in this case and that therefore RR. 266 and 267(1) may be invoked to allow the applicant to examine an officer and obtain discovery of the bank's documents, and I so direct. 13. The Rule applies to surrogate proceedings In Gow Estate (Re), 2021 ABQB 305, 2021 CarswellAlta 962, Justice Feth said: [17] Rule 2(1) of the Surrogate Rules confirms that the Civil Procedure Rules generally apply to surrogate proceedings and applications: 2. (1) The Alberta Rules of Court (AR 124/2010) apply to an application to the court if the matter is not otherwise dealt with under these Rules or the context indicates otherwise. … [38] The Personal Representatives contend that Rule 6.8 does not apply because Surrogate Rule 2 excludes the Civil Procedure Rules for a matter: a. “dealt with under these [Surrogate Rules]” or b. where “the context indicates otherwise.” [39] They argue that the Surrogate Rules only allow the disclosure of documents and questioning if a trial is ordered. I do not agree. [40] Surrogate Rule 83 authorizes the Court to set pre-trial disclosure of documents and questioning after a trial is ordered, but the Surrogate Rules are silent about pre-application disclosure and questioning prior to the hearing of an application for a proof of will trial. Since the procedure for hearing the Trial Application is not expressly “dealt with” under the Surrogate Rules, the Civil Procedure Rules are not excluded on that basis. [41] Similarly, the context does not indicate that questioning should be prohibited. The Surrogate Rules contemplate pre-trial rather than pre-application discovery, but questioning under Rule 6.8 is not discovery. The scope of the questions and any attendant document production is restricted, both by the principles regulating pre-motion questioning and the narrowed purpose of the application (i.e. to show a genuine issue to be tried, corroborated by other material evidence). [42] Surrogate Rule 64(1)(a) expressly contemplates the possibility of oral evidence for the Trial Application, although the process for collecting and presenting that evidence is not explicitly described. The Civil Procedure Rules, including Rule 6.8, are of general application and supply the necessary procedure. 14. Application for Summary Judgment The rule can be used in summary judgment applications. Having regard to the fact that the plaintiff has the onus and that it is desirable that a summary judgment should be given if there is really no reason for a trial, I would not give R. 266 the restricted meaning suggested by counsel for the defendant. … In my opinion, it would not be reasonable that in Alberta the plaintiff cannot invoke Alberta R. 266. Georges R. Brosseau Professional Corp. v. Condo Plan No. 7621095 (Owners) (1986), 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 130 at 134 (Master). 15. Crown Immunity Applies to Rule … I cannot agree that Crown immunity does not extend to R. 209 and 266 of the Alberta Rules of Court…Rutherford v. Swanson (1993), 9 Alta. L.R. (3d) 328 (Q.B.), at 333, per Bielby J.
