Admissibility of New Evidence To Be Determined at the Hearing of the Appeal In Shengli Oilfield Freet Petroleum Equipment Co. v. Ascension Virtual Group Ltd., 2010 ABQB 795, 2010 CarswellAlta 2458, 507 A.R. 188, there was an appeal from a decision of a Master, and the appellant sought to introduce new evidence at the hearing of the appeal. Though a date for the hearing of the appeal had been set, the matter came before Madam Justice Kenny to determine whether the admissibility of the new evidence had to be determined before the appeal was heard, or whether it could be decided at the time the appeal was heard. Justice Kenny put the issue in these words (paragraph 2): The Appellant seeks to introduce new evidence before the judge hearing the appeal. They propose that the judge hearing the appeal deal with the issue of whether the new evidence is admissible. The Respondents on appeal say that the new rules require that the admissibility of the evidence be determined before the matter reaches the judge hearing the appeal itself. This of course requires a two step process: one judge to review everything and determine whether the new evidence meets the threshold test set out in the rule with the second step being the hearing of the appeal itself. Her Ladyship said, at paragraph 4: … A literal reading of the section [rule 6.14] would seem to indicate that the new evidence sought to be filed and relied on in the appeal can only be filed after it is determined whether it complies with the limitation set out in the rule. This necessitates a two step process. Justice Kenny decided against the two step process, saying that “it does not appear practical to do this.” At paragraph 9, she held that … despite the wording of Rule 6.14(5)(b) and (6)(b), a two step process was not contemplated in the new rules. The new evidence will be filed and served along with the rest of the material and it will be up to the judge hearing the appeal to determine if it meets the test set out in Rule 6.14(3). In Gryckiewicz v. Ironside, 2015 ABQB 284, Justice Jeffrey gave this summary of the law relating to the admission of new evidence in an appeal from a Master: 4 Additional evidence may be admitted on an appeal from a master if the appeal judge considers it “relevant and material”: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 (the “Rules”), r 6.14(3). This is a “very lax test for such new evidence”: Boyd v Cook, 2013 ABCA 266 at para 5. The common law test for admissibility of fresh evidence in R v Palmer, [1980] 1 SCR 759, does not apply on an appeal from a master: Gudzinski Estate v Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Co, 2012 ABCA 5 at para 21. In Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 133, 2019 CarswellAlta 339, Justice Marriott had before her an appeal of an order granted by a Master granting summary judgment to the Plaintiff. The defendants filed an affidavit in support of their appeal. Her Ladyship discussed the test for receiving such additional evidence: [13] The Judge hearing an appeal from a Master's decision may consider newly submitted evidence if she or he considers that evidence “relevant and material”: Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 [Rules], r 6.14(3). The new evidence is to be filed and served along with the other appeal materials, and the judge is to make a determination on its admissibility as part of the appeal: Shengli Oilfield Freet Petroleum Equipment Co Ltd v Ascension Virtual Group Ltd, 2010 ABQB 795 (CanLII) at para 9. [14] In considering the evidentiary basis for this appeal, I refer to the decision of Hollins J. in Sewak Gill Enterprises Inc v Bedaux Real Estate Inc, 2018 ABQB 823 (CanLII). She notes that “the low threshold for the introduction of new evidence on appeal means that a true “appeal on the record” will be the exception rather than the rule”: at para 17. It is clear that the process for appeals from a Master continues to allow new evidence to be put forward on the appeal, even in the absence of an application to allow new evidence on the record being brought before the Court. [15] The Court of Appeal has made it clear that the “relevant and material” test is “a very lax test for such new evidence”: Boyd v Book, 2013 ABCA 266 (CanLII) at para 5 [Boyd]. Furthermore, “[l]ack of due diligence is not one of the tests”: Boyd at para 5. Finally “[t]his test has been applied in a broad manner, tending towards permitting evidence in rather than excluding it”: DD v Calgary Counselling Centre, 2017 ABQB 95 (CanLII) at para 26 [DD]. This Court also held that a judge can address concerns regarding the reliability of the evidence when weighing the evidence, not when dealing with admissibility: DD at para 31. Justice Marriott then discussed “self-serving” affidavits, and said: [17] The law on this issue is settled: “a self-serving affidavit is not sufficient in itself to create a triable issue in the absence of detailed facts and supporting evidence”: Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp, 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC), [1999] 3 SCR 423 [Guarantee Co] at para 31. Self-serving statements have no weight when they are “merely conclusory, argumentative, a bare assertion with no evidence supporting the claim”: Malhotra at para 33. This Court will consider the self-serving nature of any evidence when determining the weight to give it. Self-serving opinion evidence may be determined to be inadmissible: Pyrrha at para 22. That does not preclude a different determination being made at trial. … [21] Even a self-serving affidavit can raise issues that require a trial to resolve. A trial is required when the opinions and claims in the affidavit conflict with the position taken by the opposing party and those assertions by both parties are founded on the factual evidence … 2. Relevant and Material In Twinn v. Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44, 2012 CarswellAlta 104, 531 A.R. 158, Justice Browne noted that the amendments in 2011 to Rule 6.14(3) changed the test for admission of additional evidence on an appeal of a Master's decision. At paragraph 13, her Ladyship said: 13 The July 13, 2011 amendment to Rule 6.14(3) changed the test for admission of new evidence on appeal from a Master's decision. Under the new Rule 6.14(3), the party seeking admission of additional evidence is no longer required to establish due diligence, and must only show that the evidence is “relevant and material” as opposed to “prominent and noteworthy.” The facts in Gudzinski Estate v. Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Co., 2012 ABCA 5, 2012 CarswellAlta 59, 519 A.R. 215, 59 Alta. L.R. (5th) 195, were that in 2010, the parties argued the interpretation of an exclusion clause in a life insurance policy before Master Smart (2010 ABQB 638). He determined that the clause, which stated that the policy was applicable “only if your aircraft is flown by an approved pilot … who has the required license … to fly your aircraft” did not preclude coverage for the death of Mr. Gudzinski. At the time of the accidental crash that caused his death, Mr. Gudzinski had an appropriate pilot's licence, but his medical certificate had expired over a year before the accident. In 2011, Browne, J. (2011 ABQB 283, 2011 CarswellAlta 724; affirmed 2012 ABCA 5, 2012 CarswellAlta 59) found, based in part on new evidence that established that a pilot's licence is valid only for the period specified in the accompanying medical certificate, that the clause excluded coverage for Mr. Gudzinski's death. The Court of Appeal agreed with Browne J's interpretation. The Court went on to comment on issues surrounding the test for new evidence and on issues surrounding appeals from Masters under the new Rules, noting at paragraph 20 that this was one of the first such appeals to reach the Court of Appeal since the enactment of the new Rules. Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 21–24: 21 The appellant argues that the chambers judge should not have admitted the new evidence tendered by the respondent. At the time the chambers judge heard the appeal to her, the Rule provided that new evidence was admissible if it “is significant enough that it could have affected the Master's decision”. The Rule (6.14(3)) has since been amended to clarify that the new evidence must be “relevant and material”, which carries forward the previous practice under the former Rules. Rule 6.14 accordingly provides its own internal test for admitting new evidence on appeals from the Master: it must be “relevant and material”. Since the Rule contains its own test for new evidence, there is no longer room for the operation of the common-law test in R. v. Palmer[1980] 1 SCR. 759, 30 NR 181. It is inapplicable to appeals from a Master to a judge. 22 Since the new evidence here demonstrated the link between the pilot's license and the medical certificate which are central to this appeal, it clearly met the test of relevance and materiality. 23 On a related issue, the chambers judge concluded that the new Rules have changed the standard of review to be applied on appeals from the Master. While Rule 6.14 says nothing expressly about the standard of review, some case law suggests that because it specifies that appeals from the Master are “on the record”, a new standard of review is mandated. Though it is not necessary to resolve this issue in order to dispose of this appeal, dismissing this appeal should not be taken as embracing the comments on this subject in the reasons of the chambers judge. 24 It is true that new Rule 6.14 says that the appeal is “on the record”, but appeals from the Master were always “on the record”. Just because the Rule expressly states that now does not necessarily change anything. See the Interpretation Act, s 37(1)(b) (RSA 2000, c I-8). In any event, it is now imprecise to say only that appeals from the Master are “on the record”. Though the Rule states that such appeals are “on the record”, it immediately goes on to state that they are also based on any further evidence that is placed before the Queen's Bench judge on appeal. This is likewise a continuation of the previous practice. Further, where, as in this case, new evidence is put before the Queen's Bench judge, it makes no sense to say that the Master's decision on the facts should be reviewed for palpable and overriding error. The Master did not have the same evidence as the Queen's Bench judge had, which compels a fresh assessment of the facts. 3. Transcripts In Travaglione v. Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co., 2011 ABQB 604, 2011 CarswellAlta 1767, 11 C.P.C. (7th) 393, at paragraphs 36–38, Justice Shelley discussed when the requirement to file a transcript could be properly waived: 36 Rule 6.14(4)(c) requires a party appealing a Master's order to file a transcript of the proceedings before the Master, but grants the Court discretion to waive this requirement. This Rule has only been in effect since November 1, 2010, and only one case has considered it (Travaglione v. Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co., 2010 ABQB 765 (Alta. Q.B.)). That case was a decision of Veit J. in a previous appeal by Mr. Travaglione from a Master's order granting security for costs to Wawanesa and Mr. Burkinshaw. In that case, there was an issue as to the basis on which the Master granted the order. The only way to determine the basis with certainty was for Mr. Travaglione to order the transcript. Nonetheless, Veit J. decided that the transcript did not need to be produced. The content of the Notices of Motion, coupled with the fact that Mr. Travaglione was not present at the hearing before the Master, indicated that it was unlikely the Master would have proceeded on any basis other than that Mr. Travaglione resided outside Alberta. In addition, counsel before the Master also appeared before Veit J. and did not indicate that the Master proceeded on any other basis. 37 The Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, similarly requires a transcript to be filed in all appeals, and also grants the Court hearing the appeal the discretion to dismiss the requirement: “If it is necessary to do so in the interest of justice, a judge of the appellate court may give special directions and vary the rules governing the appeal book and compendium, the exhibit book, the transcript of evidence and the appellant's factum”, (R. 61.09(4). In cases decided under that Rule, courts have dispensed with the need for a transcript in situations where it was necessary for the appellant's case to be heard on the merits (Great Union Holdings Ltd. v. Palovick (2007), 221 O.A.C. 255 (Ont. Div. Ct.). However, the Ontario Court of Appeal refused to dispense with the requirement where the allegations of judicial error were solely fact based (McDowell v. Barker, 2011 CarswellOnt 1130 (Ont. C.A. [In Chambers])). The Court held that without a transcript there was no basis upon which to review the trial judge's finding. The fact that the appellant could not afford to pay for a copy of the transcript did not change the Court of Appeal's decision. 38 None of these cases provide strict guidelines on when a Court may dispense with the need for a transcript, as might be expected with a discretionary remedy. Nonetheless, the cases suggest that the Court may exercise its discretion when it is necessary for the appeal to be heard on the merits and when the absence of a transcript will not impair the Court's ability to properly hear the case. 4. Standard of Review on Appeal The Court of Appeal in Bahcheli v. Yorkton Securities Inc., 2012 ABCA 166, 2012 CarswellAlta 940, 524 A.R. 382, 65 Alta. L.R. (5th) 127 settled the matter of what the standard of review is on an appeal from a Master. Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 3, 10, 11, 16-19, and 29-30: 3 The big issue in this judgment is the standard of review on appeal from a master to a judge. Terminology is not completely consistent for the standard of review which was adopted by the Alberta Courts before the new Rules came into force. It is sometimes called non deferential, and sometimes called an appeal de novo. But more commonly the term used is “correctness”, and that has become the almost universal term since recent decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada starting with Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 SCR 235. I do not intend to distinguish among the three terms. For convenience and familiarity, I will use throughout the term “correctness”. … 10 Many Court of Queen's Bench judges have recently taken the subrule, especially the phrase “an appeal on the record” to refer to the standard of review on appeal. (See the cases cited above.) Counsel for the appellant demurs, and suggests that the phrase quoted above is merely about evidence, not about standard of review at all. I agree. 11 Appeals from Masters were always on the record, in the sense that, absent new evidence adduced for the motion, the judge had to use the evidence which the Master heard. So the new Rule made no real change: see Gudzinski Estate v Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Co., 2012 ABCA 5 (para. 24). … 16 Furthermore, the new Rules never said that an appeal from a Master was always on the record. Rule 6.14(3), quoted above, has always made an exception where the judge finds it proper to admit further evidence. That used to be a comparatively narrow exception; originally the evidence had to be arguably pivotal (to paraphrase). But since the Rule was amended in July 2011, the exception to the subrule is probably wider. In any event, it is now not ambiguous, and is not narrow. Now the proposed new evidence (referred to at the end) need only be “relevant and material” in the opinion of the judge hearing the appeal. The Rules on disclosure (discovery) have used that quoted phrase for a number of years now, and the phrase is interpreted quite broadly. Therefore, the exception to R 6.14(3) is quite wide, making the Rule that the appeal must be “on the record” rather narrow. 17 There is another important development. It is now settled law that there cannot be deference to the Master's fact findings or discretion (any need for palpable and overriding error to reverse), when the judge heard new evidence: Gudzinski v Global Allianz, supra (para. 24). 18 So far, the discussion here shows (I suggest) that the new Rules do not really dictate the standard of review on appeal from a Master. Indeed, by allowing new evidence they make a deferential standard impossible in many cases. At best, the Rules are silent. What the Standard of Review Should Be 19 That silence does not bar having a judge-made standard of review; it necessitates it. The old Rules stated no standard, but case law laid down a standard of review which held for almost a century. It was a standard of correctness, with no deference: see United Utility Workers Association v. TransAlta Corp., 2004 ABCA 200, 354 AR 58 (para. 20); Willman v Administrator of Motor Vehicle Claims Act (1979) 17 AR 608 (para. 12) (CA). … 29 So there would be a number of dangers in making the standard of review deferential (or doing so in some circumstances). Counsel for the appellant asked us what was broken which needs fixing? He said that appeals from Masters worked well for 90 years, and I believe that he is correct. 30 In my view, the standard of review on appeal from a Master to a judge, on all issues, is still correctness. In Coley v. Payne, 2015 ABQB 269, at paragraphs 4–7, Justice Read concluded that the pre-Bahcheli decision of Dagher v. Thompson, 2011 ABQB 499 in which Park, J. described the standard of review for decisions which involved the exercise of a Master's discretion as one of reasonableness, has been supplanted by Bahcheli. The standard of review of any Master's decision is correctness. In Kulaga v. First National Financial GP Corp., 2014 ABQB 400, 2014 CarswellAlta 1086, Justice McCarthy gave this summary of the law relating to the standard of review in an appeal from a Master (at paragraphs 13–19): 13 Both parties have identified that the standard of review for an appeal of a Master's decision is correctness, based on Bahcheli v Yorkton Securities Inc., 2012 ABCA 166 at para 30: “In my view, the standard of review on appeal from a Master to a judge, on all issues, is still correctness.” Additionally, an appeal from a Master's decision pursuant to Rule 6.14 of the Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, is a hearing de novo, as found by Justice Bensler in P. Burns Resources Limited v Locke, Stock & Barrel Company Ltd., 2013 ABQB 129: “An appeal from a Master's decision is a de novo hearing and the standard of review is one of correctness … The Judge may exercise any discretion anew and substitute their own views for that of the Master.” 14 In Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111, the standard of review for appeals from a Master's decision was reviewed. Specifically, the Court reviewed the Supreme Court's decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, and its impact on the standard of review for summary judgment decisions involving a Master. 15 Hyrniak was an appeal based on Rule 20 of the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194. In 2010, Rule 20 was revamped to allow a limited weighing of evidence in summary judgment procedures: Rules of Civil Procedure, supra, r 20.04(2.1). The context of Rule 20 differs from Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court. 16 Rule 7.3(1) of the Rules of Court states: 7.3. (1) A party may apply to the Court for summary judgment in respect of all or part of a claim on one or more of the following grounds: (a) there is no defence to a claim or part of it; (b) there is no merit to a claim or part of it; (c) the only real issue is the amount to be awarded. 17 In Orr, the Court concluded at para 20: The Supreme Court's direction in Hryniak v. Mauldin regarding the deference to be shown to the motions judge on an application under Ontario's Rule 20 for summary judgment therefore does not apply to first-instance decisions on applications for summary judgment brought under Alberta's Rule 7.3—irrespective of whether that decision was taken by a master or a judge—for summary judgment. It does, however, apply to decisions on applications for judgment by way of a summary trial under Alberta's Rule 7.5 (which decisions must always be taken by a judge, and not a master). 18 Master Mason recently summarized the difference between Ontario's Rule 20 and Alberta's Rule 7.3 in Whitecourt Power Limited Partnership v Interpro Technical Services Ltd, 2014 ABQB 135 at para 35: The focus of the Court's reasons in Hryniak v. Mauldin is Ontario's two-stage approach to summary judgment contained in rules 20.04(2) and 20.04(2.1-2.2). The first stage is similar to Alberta's rule 7.3. The recently added second stage involves the discretionary use of enhanced fact-finding powers to weigh the evidence, evaluate the credibility of a deponent, draw any reasonable inference from the evidence, and order the presentation of oral evidence. This second stage is not found in Alberta rule 7.3, but as pointed out by Brown J. in Orr v. Fort McKay First Nation at paragraph 19, is broadly comparable to an application by way of summary trial under Alberta rule 7.5. 19 Recently, in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108, the Court of Appeal applied Hryniak to Rule 7.3, which has effectively modernized the test for summary judgment. However, in my view, the standard of review remains the same. An appeal from a Master's decision is a de novo hearing and the standard of review is correctness. In HOOPP Realty Inc. v. Emery Jamieson LLP, 2020 ABCA 159, 2020 CarswellAlta 748, 5 Alta. L.R. (7th) 213, 11 C.L.R. (4th) 203, [2020] 7 W.W.R. 187, the Court of Appeal said: [41] Where an appeal from a master's decision to a chambers judge involves the same record and the same submissions, it is not an error for a chambers judge to summarily describe his or her analysis and conclusions with reference to the master's decision if he or she otherwise finds that it was correct in fact and law. In taking this approach, the chambers judge here did not defer to the masters' decision or apply any other standard of review. This procedure was followed by Justice Price in Zulu Publications Inc. v. WestJet Airlines Ltd., 2021 ABQB 629, 2021 CarswellAlta 1884 at para. 4. In Sewak Gill Enterprises Inc. v. Bedaux Real Estate Inc., 2018 ABQB 823, 2018 CarswellAlta 2122, Justice Hollins did not agree that an appeal from a Master is de novo. Her Ladyship said: [15] An appeal from the Master is often described to and by this Court as an appeal de novo notwithstanding that the wording of Rule 6.14(3) clearly describes it as an appeal “on the record”. The continuing description of these appeals as de novo in the face of a Rule that says otherwise seems to trace back to the decision of Cote, JA in Bahcheli v. Yorkton Securities, 2012 ABCA 166 (CanLII) where he said: The big issue in this judgment is the standard of review on appeal from a master to a judge. Terminology is not completely consistent for the standard of review which was adopted by the Alberta Courts before the new Rules came into force. It is sometimes called non-deferential, and sometimes called an appeal de novo. But more commonly the term used is “correctness”… ; para.3. [16] It should be noted that Justice Cote's reasons were expressly directed to the standard of review—now settled to be correctness—and not to the permissible evidentiary basis, or more plainly, the mechanics of these appeals. In fact, he clearly distinguishes the standard of review on appeal from the evidence considered on appeal at paragraph 10 of his Reasons. These concepts, while separate, are obviously linked and that was, in fact, Justice Cote's point; if the appellant has the ability to amplify the record from below and the appeal is thus based on something different than the evidence before the Master, the standard of review cannot be higher than correctness. [17] With respect to my colleagues, I do not read Justice Cote's words as saying that an appeal from the Master to our Court is an automatically an appeal de novo but rather that the low threshold for the introduction of new evidence on appeal[1] means that a true “appeal on the record” will be the exception rather than the rule. [18] Because appellants can amplify the record relatively easily and because the standard of review is correctness which does not require deference to the Master's decision, I agree that it looks less like an appeal on the record and more like an appeal de novo. But it is not. [19] Black's Law Dictionary defines an appeal de novo as “a new hearing of a matter, conducted as if the original hearing had not taken place”. That does not properly describe appeals from the Masters. In addition to the clear wording of the Rule, I say this for the following reasons: a) There would be no reason to speak of any standard of review at all if the appeal were truly de novo; b) Rule 6.14 still contains a test, albeit relatively easily satisfied, for adding new evidence to the record before the Master, which would be moot if the appeal were truly de novo; and c) If the appeal were truly de novo, I could ignore the proceedings before the Master, including the Transcript of Proceedings which appellants are obligated to provide. Further, I could also ignore the Masters' reasoning completely which is different than saying that he or she was correct. Her Ladyship made the same points in Prestige Granite & Marble Inc. v. Maillot Homes Inc., 2018 ABQB 1040, 2018 CarswellAlta 3182 at paragraphs 4–7, and in Steer v. Chicago Title Insurance Company, 2019 ABQB 318, 2019 CarswellAlta 850, 88 C.L.R. (4th) 25, 1 R.P.R. (6th) 51, [2019] I.L.R. I-6157 at paragraphs 6–10. In Savanna Well Servicing Inc. v. Cleo Energy Corp., 2023 ABKB 595, Justice Neufeld explained the standard of review in these words: [2] Appeals of Applications Judge decisions are adjudicated on a standard of review of correctness. They are considered de novo hearings, in which new evidence may be tendered. That is not to say that the Applications Judge decision is to be ignored or discarded, especially when no new evidence is presented, and the decision below is issued with detailed reasons, as is the case here. The decision can and often will provide an appropriate framework of analysis for examining whether, based on the record, the Applications Judge was correct: Boyko v Boyko, ABQB 266 at para 5. The correctness review is undertaken with a view to determining whether the decision of the Applications Judge contains material misapprehensions of fact, errors of reasoning or outcomes that are clearly wrong: Canuck v Yangarra, 2022 ABQB 145 at para 36. 5. Appeal from Application Judge’s Costs Order Some cases decided under the old Rules, suggested that the policy reasons underlying the rule which requires leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal a costs order made by the Court of Queen’s Bench (as it then was) should apply to appeals from costs orders of Masters (as they were then known). However, in Coley v. Payne, 2015 ABQB 269, 2015 CarswellAlta 2299, Justice Read, addressing the issue after the current rules came into effect, disagreed, and said: [9] In their written materials, the Respondents argued that Rule 505(3) applies to this appeal and so appeals on costs may only proceed with leave of the court “giving the judgment or making the order”. They relied upon Oxford Properties Group Inc. v. Lymer 2005 ABQB 305 in support. Again, however, at the hearing, the Respondents were prepared to concede that no leave was necessary. [10] I agree. Rule 505(3) applies only to appeals to the Court of Appeal. Lymer relied upon by the Respondents, does say that the Rule ought to apply to appeals to this Court as well but cites no authority for this, indicating only that “common sense would dictate that [the Rule] would apply to a Master’s decision on costs, just as it applies to a Judge’s decision on costs” (at para 25). [11] I am not persuaded that is correct. I note that in Vegreville Electrical Services (1996) Ltd. v. 695093 Alberta Ltd. (1998), 1998 ABQB 517 (CanLII), 239 A.R. 396, cited in Lymer, Veit, J. does not conclude that R. 505(3) applies to appeals from a master to this Court and, indeed, seems to imply the opposite: “there is no rule which requires leave of the Master before a costs decision is appealed to the court” (para 5). [12] In any event, Lymer was decided under the previous Rules of Court, now repealed and I decline to follow it. The new rules operate on the foundational principle that they should be interpreted so that disputes can be resolved in a timely and cost effective manner (see rule 1.2). A requirement that leave be obtained would impose a further unnecessary step to appeals from masters and increase costs. I find that no leave to appeal is necessary.

Self-serving statements have no weight when they are “merely conclusory, argumentative, a bare assertion with no evidence supporting the claim”: Malhotra at para 33.
This Court will consider the self-serving nature of any evidence when determining the weight to give it.
Self-serving opinion evidence may be determined to be inadmissible: Pyrrha at para 22.
That does not preclude a different determination being made at trial. … [21] Even a self-serving affidavit can raise issues that require a trial to resolve.
A trial is required when the opinions and claims in the affidavit conflict with the position taken by the opposing party and those assertions by both parties are founded on the factual evidence … 2.
Relevant and Material In Twinn v.
Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44, 2012 CarswellAlta 104, 531 A.R.
158, Justice Browne noted that the amendments in 2011 to Rule 6.14(3) changed the test for admission of additional evidence on an appeal of a Master's decision.
At paragraph 13, her Ladyship said: 13 The July 13, 2011 amendment to Rule 6.14(3) changed the test for admission of new evidence on appeal from a Master's decision.

Under the new Rule 6.14(3), the party seeking admission of additional evidence is no longer required to establish due diligence, and must only show that the evidence is “relevant and material” as opposed to “prominent and noteworthy.” The facts in Gudzinski Estate v.
Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Co., 2012 ABCA 5, 2012 CarswellAlta 59, 519 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 195, were that in 2010, the parties argued the interpretation of an exclusion clause in a life insurance policy before Master Smart (2010 ABQB 638).

He determined that the clause, which stated that the policy was applicable “only if your aircraft is flown by an approved pilot … who has the required license … to fly your aircraft” did not preclude coverage for the death of Mr.
Gudzinski.
At the time of the accidental crash that caused his death, Mr.
Gudzinski had an appropriate pilot's licence, but his medical certificate had expired over a year before the accident.
In 2011, Browne, J.

(2011 ABQB 283, 2011 CarswellAlta 724; affirmed 2012 ABCA 5, 2012 CarswellAlta 59) found, based in part on new evidence that established that a pilot's licence is valid only for the period specified in the accompanying medical certificate, that the clause excluded coverage for Mr.
Gudzinski's death.
The Court of Appeal agreed with Browne J's interpretation.

The Court went on to comment on issues surrounding the test for new evidence and on issues surrounding appeals from Masters under the new Rules, noting at paragraph 20 that this was one of the first such appeals to reach the Court of Appeal since the enactment of the new Rules.
Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 21–24: 21 The appellant argues that the chambers judge should not have admitted the new evidence tendered by the respondent.
At the time the chambers judge heard the appeal to her, the Rule provided that new evidence was admissible if it “is significant enough that it could have affected the Master's decision”.
The Rule (6.14(3)) has since been amended to clarify that the new evidence must be “relevant and material”, which carries forward the previous practice under the former Rules.
Rule 6.14 accordingly provides its own internal test for admitting new evidence on appeals from the Master: it must be “relevant and material”.
Since the Rule contains its own test for new evidence, there is no longer room for the operation of the common-law test in R. v.
Palmer[1980] 1 SCR.
It is inapplicable to appeals from a Master to a judge.
22 Since the new evidence here demonstrated the link between the pilot's license and the medical certificate which are central to this appeal, it clearly met the test of relevance and materiality.
23 On a related issue, the chambers judge concluded that the new Rules have changed the standard of review to be applied on appeals from the Master.

While Rule 6.14 says nothing expressly about the standard of review, some case law suggests that because it specifies that appeals from the Master are “on the record”, a new standard of review is mandated.

Though it is not necessary to resolve this issue in order to dispose of this appeal, dismissing this appeal should not be taken as embracing the comments on this subject in the reasons of the chambers judge.
24 It is true that new Rule 6.14 says that the appeal is “on the record”, but appeals from the Master were always “on the record”.
Just because the Rule expressly states that now does not necessarily change anything.
See the Interpretation Act, s 37(1)(b) (RSA 2000, c I-8).
In any event, it is now imprecise to say only that appeals from the Master are “on the record”.
Though the Rule states that such appeals are “on the record”, it immediately goes on to state that they are also based on any further evidence that is placed before the Queen's Bench judge on appeal.
This is likewise a continuation of the previous practice.

Further, where, as in this case, new evidence is put before the Queen's Bench judge, it makes no sense to say that the Master's decision on the facts should be reviewed for palpable and overriding error.
The Master did not have the same evidence as the Queen's Bench judge had, which compels a fresh assessment of the facts.
Transcripts In Travaglione v.
Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co., 2011 ABQB 604, 2011 CarswellAlta 1767, 11 C.P.C.

(7th) 393, at paragraphs 36–38, Justice Shelley discussed when the requirement to file a transcript could be properly waived: 36 Rule 6.14(4)(c) requires a party appealing a Master's order to file a transcript of the proceedings before the Master, but grants the Court discretion to waive this requirement.
This Rule has only been in effect since November 1, 2010, and only one case has considered it (Travaglione v.
Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Co., 2010 ABQB 765 (Alta.
That case was a decision of Veit J. in a previous appeal by Mr.
Travaglione from a Master's order granting security for costs to Wawanesa and Mr.
Burkinshaw.
In that case, there was an issue as to the basis on which the Master granted the order.
The only way to determine the basis with certainty was for Mr.
Travaglione to order the transcript.
Nonetheless, Veit J. decided that the transcript did not need to be produced.
The content of the Notices of Motion, coupled with the fact that Mr.
Travaglione was not present at the hearing before the Master, indicated that it was unlikely the Master would have proceeded on any basis other than that Mr.
Travaglione resided outside Alberta.
In addition, counsel before the Master also appeared before Veit J. and did not indicate that the Master proceeded on any other basis.
37 The Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O.

194, similarly requires a transcript to be filed in all appeals, and also grants the Court hearing the appeal the discretion to dismiss the requirement: “If it is necessary to do so in the interest of justice, a judge of the appellate court may give special directions and vary the rules governing the appeal book and compendium, the exhibit book, the transcript of evidence and the appellant's factum”, (R.

In cases decided under that Rule, courts have dispensed with the need for a transcript in situations where it was necessary for the appellant's case to be heard on the merits (Great Union Holdings Ltd. v.
Palovick (2007), 221 O.A.C.
Div.
Ct.).
However, the Ontario Court of Appeal refused to dispense with the requirement where the allegations of judicial error were solely fact based (McDowell v.
Barker, 2011 CarswellOnt 1130 (Ont.
C.A.
[In Chambers])).
The Court held that without a transcript there was no basis upon which to review the trial judge's finding.
The fact that the appellant could not afford to pay for a copy of the transcript did not change the Court of Appeal's decision.
38 None of these cases provide strict guidelines on when a Court may dispense with the need for a transcript, as might be expected with a discretionary remedy.

Nonetheless, the cases suggest that the Court may exercise its discretion when it is necessary for the appeal to be heard on the merits and when the absence of a transcript will not impair the Court's ability to properly hear the case.
Standard of Review on Appeal The Court of Appeal in Bahcheli v.
Yorkton Securities Inc., 2012 ABCA 166, 2012 CarswellAlta 940, 524 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 127 settled the matter of what the standard of review is on an appeal from a Master.
Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 3, 10, 11, 16-19, and 29-30: 3 The big issue in this judgment is the standard of review on appeal from a master to a judge.
Terminology is not completely consistent for the standard of review which was adopted by the Alberta Courts before the new Rules came into force.
It is sometimes called non deferential, and sometimes called an appeal de novo.
But more commonly the term used is “correctness”, and that has become the almost universal term since recent decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada starting with Housen v.
Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 SCR 235.
I do not intend to distinguish among the three terms.

For convenience and familiarity, I will use throughout the term “correctness”. … 10 Many Court of Queen's Bench judges have recently taken the subrule, especially the phrase “an appeal on the record” to refer to the standard of review on appeal.
(See the cases cited above.) Counsel for the appellant demurs, and suggests that the phrase quoted above is merely about evidence, not about standard of review at all.
I agree.
11 Appeals from Masters were always on the record, in the sense that, absent new evidence adduced for the motion, the judge had to use the evidence which the Master heard.
So the new Rule made no real change: see Gudzinski Estate v Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Co., 2012 ABCA 5 (para.
24). … 16 Furthermore, the new Rules never said that an appeal from a Master was always on the record.
Rule 6.14(3), quoted above, has always made an exception where the judge finds it proper to admit further evidence.
That used to be a comparatively narrow exception; originally the evidence had to be arguably pivotal (to paraphrase).
But since the Rule was amended in July 2011, the exception to the subrule is probably wider.
In any event, it is now not ambiguous, and is not narrow.
Now the proposed new evidence (referred to at the end) need only be “relevant and material” in the opinion of the judge hearing the appeal.
The Rules on disclosure (discovery) have used that quoted phrase for a number of years now, and the phrase is interpreted quite broadly.
Therefore, the exception to R 6.14(3) is quite wide, making the Rule that the appeal must be “on the record” rather narrow.
17 There is another important development.

It is now settled law that there cannot be deference to the Master's fact findings or discretion (any need for palpable and overriding error to reverse), when the judge heard new evidence: Gudzinski v Global Allianz, supra (para.
18 So far, the discussion here shows (I suggest) that the new Rules do not really dictate the standard of review on appeal from a Master.
Indeed, by allowing new evidence they make a deferential standard impossible in many cases.
At best, the Rules are silent.
What the Standard of Review Should Be 19 That silence does not bar having a judge-made standard of review; it necessitates it.
The old Rules stated no standard, but case law laid down a standard of review which held for almost a century.
It was a standard of correctness, with no deference: see United Utility Workers Association v.
TransAlta Corp., 2004 ABCA 200, 354 AR 58 (para.
20); Willman v Administrator of Motor Vehicle Claims Act (1979) 17 AR 608 (para.
12) (CA). … 29 So there would be a number of dangers in making the standard of review deferential (or doing so in some circumstances).
Counsel for the appellant asked us what was broken which needs fixing?
He said that appeals from Masters worked well for 90 years, and I believe that he is correct.
30 In my view, the standard of review on appeal from a Master to a judge, on all issues, is still correctness.
In Coley v.
Payne, 2015 ABQB 269, at paragraphs 4–7, Justice Read concluded that the pre-Bahcheli decision of Dagher v.

Thompson, 2011 ABQB 499 in which Park, J. described the standard of review for decisions which involved the exercise of a Master's discretion as one of reasonableness, has been supplanted by Bahcheli.
The standard of review of any Master's decision is correctness.
In Kulaga v.

First National Financial GP Corp., 2014 ABQB 400, 2014 CarswellAlta 1086, Justice McCarthy gave this summary of the law relating to the standard of review in an appeal from a Master (at paragraphs 13–19): 13 Both parties have identified that the standard of review for an appeal of a Master's decision is correctness, based on Bahcheli v Yorkton Securities Inc., 2012 ABCA 166 at para 30: “In my view, the standard of review on appeal from a Master to a judge, on all issues, is still correctness.” Additionally, an appeal from a Master's decision pursuant to Rule 6.14 of the Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, is a hearing de novo, as found by Justice Bensler in P.

Burns Resources Limited v Locke, Stock & Barrel Company Ltd., 2013 ABQB 129: “An appeal from a Master's decision is a de novo hearing and the standard of review is one of correctness … The Judge may exercise any discretion anew and substitute their own views for that of the Master.” 14 In Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111, the standard of review for appeals from a Master's decision was reviewed.
Specifically, the Court reviewed the Supreme Court's decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, and its impact on the standard of review for summary judgment decisions involving a Master.
15 Hyrniak was an appeal based on Rule 20 of the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194.
In 2010, Rule 20 was revamped to allow a limited weighing of evidence in summary judgment procedures: Rules of Civil Procedure, supra, r 20.04(2.1).
The context of Rule 20 differs from Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court.
16 Rule 7.3(1) of the Rules of Court states: 7.3.
(1) A party may apply to the Court for summary judgment in respect of all or part of a claim on one or more of the following grounds:
(a) there is no defence to a claim or part of it
(b) there is no merit to a claim or part of it
(c) the only real issue is the amount to be awarded.
17 In Orr, the Court concluded at para 20: The Supreme Court's direction in Hryniak v.

Mauldin regarding the deference to be shown to the motions judge on an application under Ontario's Rule 20 for summary judgment therefore does not apply to first-instance decisions on applications for summary judgment brought under Alberta's Rule 7.3—irrespective of whether that decision was taken by a master or a judge—for summary judgment.
It does, however, apply to decisions on applications for judgment by way of a summary trial under Alberta's Rule 7.5 (which decisions must always be taken by a judge, and not a master).

18 Master Mason recently summarized the difference between Ontario's Rule 20 and Alberta's Rule 7.3 in Whitecourt Power Limited Partnership v Interpro Technical Services Ltd, 2014 ABQB 135 at para 35: The focus of the Court's reasons in Hryniak v.
Mauldin is Ontario's two-stage approach to summary judgment contained in rules 20.04(2) and 20.04(2.1-2.2).
The first stage is similar to Alberta's rule 7.3.

The recently added second stage involves the discretionary use of enhanced fact-finding powers to weigh the evidence, evaluate the credibility of a deponent, draw any reasonable inference from the evidence, and order the presentation of oral evidence.
This second stage is not found in Alberta rule 7.3, but as pointed out by Brown J. in Orr v.
Fort McKay First Nation at paragraph 19, is broadly comparable to an application by way of summary trial under Alberta rule 7.5.
19 Recently, in Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108, the Court of Appeal applied Hryniak to Rule 7.3, which has effectively modernized the test for summary judgment.
However, in my view, the standard of review remains the same.
An appeal from a Master's decision is a de novo hearing and the standard of review is correctness.
In HOOPP Realty Inc. v.
Emery Jamieson LLP, 2020 ABCA 159, 2020 CarswellAlta 748, 5 Alta.
L.R.

187, the Court of Appeal said: [41] Where an appeal from a master's decision to a chambers judge involves the same record and the same submissions, it is not an error for a chambers judge to summarily describe his or her analysis and conclusions with reference to the master's decision if he or she otherwise finds that it was correct in fact and law.
In taking this approach, the chambers judge here did not defer to the masters' decision or apply any other standard of review.
This procedure was followed by Justice Price in Zulu Publications Inc. v.
WestJet Airlines Ltd., 2021 ABQB 629, 2021 CarswellAlta 1884 at para.
In Sewak Gill Enterprises Inc. v.
Bedaux Real Estate Inc., 2018 ABQB 823, 2018 CarswellAlta 2122, Justice Hollins did not agree that an appeal from a Master is de novo.

Her Ladyship said: [15] An appeal from the Master is often described to and by this Court as an appeal de novo notwithstanding that the wording of Rule 6.14(3) clearly describes it as an appeal “on the record”.
The continuing description of these appeals as de novo in the face of a Rule that says otherwise seems to trace back to the decision of Cote, JA in Bahcheli v.
Yorkton Securities, 2012 ABCA 166 (CanLII) where he said: The big issue in this judgment is the standard of review on appeal from a master to a judge.
Terminology is not completely consistent for the standard of review which was adopted by the Alberta Courts before the new Rules came into force.
It is sometimes called non-deferential, and sometimes called an appeal de novo.
But more commonly the term used is “correctness”… ; para.3.

[16] It should be noted that Justice Cote's reasons were expressly directed to the standard of review—now settled to be correctness—and not to the permissible evidentiary basis, or more plainly, the mechanics of these appeals.
In fact, he clearly distinguishes the standard of review on appeal from the evidence considered on appeal at paragraph 10 of his Reasons.

These concepts, while separate, are obviously linked and that was, in fact, Justice Cote's point; if the appellant has the ability to amplify the record from below and the appeal is thus based on something different than the evidence before the Master, the standard of review cannot be higher than correctness.

[17] With respect to my colleagues, I do not read Justice Cote's words as saying that an appeal from the Master to our Court is an automatically an appeal de novo but rather that the low threshold for the introduction of new evidence on appeal[1] means that a true “appeal on the record” will be the exception rather than the rule.

[18] Because appellants can amplify the record relatively easily and because the standard of review is correctness which does not require deference to the Master's decision, I agree that it looks less like an appeal on the record and more like an appeal de novo.
But it is not.
[19] Black's Law Dictionary defines an appeal de novo as “a new hearing of a matter, conducted as if the original hearing had not taken place”.
That does not properly describe appeals from the Masters.

In addition to the clear wording of the Rule, I say this for the following reasons: a) There would be no reason to speak of any standard of review at all if the appeal were truly de novo; b) Rule 6.14 still contains a test, albeit relatively easily satisfied, for adding new evidence to the record before the Master, which would be moot if the appeal were truly de novo; and c) If the appeal were truly de novo, I could ignore the proceedings before the Master, including the Transcript of Proceedings which appellants are obligated to provide.
Further, I could also ignore the Masters' reasoning completely which is different than saying that he or she was correct.
Her Ladyship made the same points in Prestige Granite & Marble Inc. v.
Maillot Homes Inc., 2018 ABQB 1040, 2018 CarswellAlta 3182 at paragraphs 4–7, and in Steer v.
Chicago Title Insurance Company, 2019 ABQB 318, 2019 CarswellAlta 850, 88 C.L.R.
I-6157 at paragraphs 6–10.
In Savanna Well Servicing Inc. v.
Cleo Energy Corp., 2023 ABKB 595, Justice Neufeld explained the standard of review in these words: [2] Appeals of Applications Judge decisions are adjudicated on a standard of review of correctness.
They are considered de novo hearings, in which new evidence may be tendered.

That is not to say that the Applications Judge decision is to be ignored or discarded, especially when no new evidence is presented, and the decision below is issued with detailed reasons, as is the case here.
The decision can and often will provide an appropriate framework of analysis for examining whether, based on the record, the Applications Judge was correct: Boyko v Boyko, ABQB 266 at para 5.

The correctness review is undertaken with a view to determining whether the decision of the Applications Judge contains material misapprehensions of fact, errors of reasoning or outcomes that are clearly wrong: Canuck v Yangarra, 2022 ABQB 145 at para 36.

Appeal from Application Judge’s Costs Order Some cases decided under the old Rules, suggested that the policy reasons underlying the rule which requires leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal a costs order made by the Court of Queen’s Bench (as it then was) should apply to appeals from costs orders of Masters (as they were then known).
However, in Coley v.

Payne, 2015 ABQB 269, 2015 CarswellAlta 2299, Justice Read, addressing the issue after the current rules came into effect, disagreed, and said: [9] In their written materials, the Respondents argued that Rule 505(3) applies to this appeal and so appeals on costs may only proceed with leave of the court “giving the judgment or making the order”.
They relied upon Oxford Properties Group Inc. v.
Lymer 2005 ABQB 305 in support.
Again, however, at the hearing, the Respondents were prepared to concede that no leave was necessary.
[10] I agree.
Rule 505(3) applies only to appeals to the Court of Appeal.

Lymer relied upon by the Respondents, does say that the Rule ought to apply to appeals to this Court as well but cites no authority for this, indicating only that “common sense would dictate that [the Rule] would apply to a Master’s decision on costs, just as it applies to a Judge’s decision on costs” (at para 25).
[11] I am not persuaded that is correct.
I note that in Vegreville Electrical Services (1996) Ltd. v.
695093 Alberta Ltd.
396, cited in Lymer, Veit, J. does not conclude that R.

505(3) applies to appeals from a master to this Court and, indeed, seems to imply the opposite: “there is no rule which requires leave of the Master before a costs decision is appealed to the court” (para 5).
[12] In any event, Lymer was decided under the previous Rules of Court, now repealed and I decline to follow it.
The new rules operate on the foundational principle that they should be interpreted so that disputes can be resolved in a timely and cost effective manner (see rule 1.2).
A requirement that leave be obtained would impose a further unnecessary step to appeals from masters and increase costs.
I find that no leave to appeal is necessary.

paragraphs.text: (1) A notice of appointment for questioning must (a) specify a reasonable date, time and place for the appointment for questioning, (b) describe any records the person is required to bring to the appointment for questioning, and (c) request the person to be questioned to specify any arrangements necessary to accommodate the person's reasonable needs which, to the extent reasonably possible, must be accommodated. (2) The notice of appointment for questioning must be served 5 days or more before the appointment date (a) on the person to be questioned, or if a lawyer acts for that person, on the lawyer, and (b) on each of the other parties. (3) On application, the Court may resolve a dispute over the date, time, place and person to be questioned and any related matters, and the records to be produced at the appointment for questioning. (4) The attendance of a person to be questioned and the records to be produced at the appointment for questioning may be required by an order under rule 6.38.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 6.17:1 Rule 6.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 6.17. Payment of Allowance In Nickol v. McKay Bros. Farm Implements Ltd. (1995), 26 Alta. L.R. (3d) 355 (Master), Master Alberstat considered the proper amount to be paid as conduct money for the production of a witness for cross-examination. The plaintiff had commenced the action in Lethbridge and the defendant brought an application to strike the claim. The affiant swore the supporting affidavit in the defendant's Western Canada office in Regina. The applicant/defendant submitted that the proper conduct money should cover the cost of travelling from Regina to Lethbridge. The respondent/plaintiff submitted that only the cost of travel from Edmonton (the location of the registered attorney of the defendant) to Lethbridge should be covered. Master Alberstat disagreed with both positions and ordered conduct money as if the affiant's residence was Lethbridge. At pp. 358-59, the learned Master said: If an applicant in making an interlocutory is required to prove his or her allegations with evidence from a witness, whether that witness is from Regina or Hong Kong that applicant must be prepared to produce that witness to be examined. If the respondent on such an application wishes to cross-examine that witness why should the respondent pay to bring the witness to the place of trial to be cross-examined? If an applicant who initiates an application wishes to support the application with an affidavit of an officer from its head office or branch office or anywhere on the globe then that applicant should be prepared to present that affiant to be cross-examined as to the truth of his statements in the affidavit. If it were otherwise a wealthy litigant could financially exhaust an opponent by making interlocutory applications supported by affidavits from corporate officers from around the globe. This of course is an exaggeration but it should illustrate what I think is only fair, and that is, simply, that he who uses a witness's evidence in an interlocutory matter should be prepared to present that witness for cross-examination at the place of trial. In this particular case I therefore exercise the court's discretion and direct that the conduct money to be paid to the affiant shall be the amount required as if the affiant's residence was in Lethbridge, Alberta. Mr. Justice Miller, in Canada (Attorney General) v. Sandford (1995), 34 Alta. L.R. (3d) 170 (Q.B.), considered the matter of the conduct money to be paid in order to cross-examine an affiant. He canvassed the law on the area and modified the comments of Master Alberstat in Nickol v. McKay Bros. Farm Implements Ltd., At pp. 174-79, his Lordship said: The second question is what should be the proper amount of the conduct money that the defendant should remit in advance to the plaintiff for the opportunity to examine this affiant? There are two lines of decided cases in Alberta dealing with this area of interpretation of our Rules of Court. The one which the plaintiff puts forward, and which was followed by Master Quinn, is best expressed in the decision of Master Breitkreuz in the case of F.G. Bradley Co. v. Maxwell Taylor's Restaurants Inc. It is certainly broad enough to encompass the “head office” approach on one end of the spectrum and Master Alberstat's approach at the other end. In my view, if Master Alberstat is suggesting that R. 314(4) invariably means that if the litigating party chooses an affiant who resides somewhere other than the place where the trial is to be held no conduct money is properly payable, then I think this goes too far, for it fetters the court's discretion too much in that direction. The courts discretion in setting the amount of conduct money should not be fettered in any way. There can be no definitive rule. paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.18 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: (1) If a lawyer is served with a notice of appointment for questioning and an allowance is also paid, the lawyer must, (a) as soon as practicable, inform the person to be questioned about the appointment, and (b) use the allowance only for the purpose for which it is paid. (2) If a person to be questioned does not attend the appointment for questioning, the allowance must, unless the parties otherwise agree or the Court otherwise orders, be repaid to the person who paid it by (a) the lawyer, or (b) if the lawyer paid the allowance to another person, that other person.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.19 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: (1) If a person to be questioned will not be able to understand the questions or be able to answer the questions without the aid of an interpreter, the person to be questioned must give reasonable notice of that fact to the party who served the notice of appointment for questioning, and the questioning party must then notify every other party that an interpreter will be present. (2) The questioning party must provide an interpreter (a) who is impartial and competent, and (b) who takes an oath to interpret the questions and answers correctly and honestly. (3) The cost of the interpreter must initially be borne by the questioning party.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 6.20 – Part 6. Resolving Issues And Preserving Rights
paragraphs.text: (1) A person questioned on an affidavit under this Part or a person questioned as a witness for the purpose of obtaining a transcript under this Part for use at a hearing may also be questioned by any other party, and the person questioned may then be questioned again by the questioning party on that person's answers to the questions of other parties. (2) Questioning and questioning again under this rule by parties adverse in interest may take the form of cross-examination. (3) The questions and answers must be recorded word for word by a person qualified to do so (a) by a method that is capable of producing a written transcript, and (b) in a manner agreed on by the parties or directed by the Court. (4) The person recording the oral questioning must (a) keep in safe custody the recorded questioning, (b) if required to do so, honestly and accurately transcribe the recorded questioning and deliver a copy of the transcript, as required, and (c) on or attached to any transcript (i) state the person's name, (ii) specify the date and place where the questioning occurred, and (iii) certify the transcript, or the portion of the questioning transcribed, as complete and accurate. (5) The questioning party must (a) make necessary arrangements for the questioning to be recorded, and (b) file the transcript unless the Court otherwise orders. (6) A person is qualified to record and transcribe oral questioning under this Part if the person is (a) an official court reporter, (b) a person appointed by the Court as an examiner under the Alberta Rules of Court (Alta. Reg. 390/68), or (c) a shorthand writer, sworn to record the questioning word for word and to impartially fulfil the duties imposed by subrule (4), who (i) is an agent or employee of an official court reporter, or (ii) has been approved by the parties.
